Then you play with two, and next week they bring friends. Word spreads fast among children, especially when it's fun.
I'll make a small poster for the notice board.
That's a good start. Keep it bright and short, with time and place in big letters.
The teacher said I should speak louder, but I feel shy when everyone looks at me.
It's something many students work on. Try speaking to one friendly face in the room instead of the whole class.
I can try that.
Also, practise at home reading a paragraph aloud from a distance. Slowly raise your volume, until it's comfortable for someone across the room to hear you.
My little cousin asked me why the moon follows our car. I had no good answer.
That's a charming question. The moon is so far away that when we move a short distance, it appears to stay in the same place in the sky, so it looks like it is following us.
So it's not really following?
No. Trees and buildings near the road seem to rush past, but the moon is too far for that to change, so it appears to keep up with you.
My friend and I always meet at the same cafe, and I'd like to suggest a change.
A change is refreshing. Do you have a new place in mind?
A tea stall near the lake.
That sounds nice. Say, 'I've been wanting to try the tea stall near the lake. Shall we go this Saturday?' Make it sound like an adventure, not a complaint.
What if she doesn't like it?
Then you've both learned something, and you can alternate places. The point is to enjoy time together.
She agreed. Should I pick the day or let her?
Offer two options, like Saturday or Sunday afternoon, so it's easy for her to choose.
Saturday, then. I'll text her now.
A short message with the time and place is all you need.
I bought a mango that looks ripe, but it's hard. When will it be ready?
Mangoes ripen at room temperature. A hard one might need two to four days. You can speed it up by keeping it in a paper bag with a banana.
Why does the banana help?
Ripe bananas give off a gas called ethylene, which makes other fruit ripen faster. The paper bag holds that gas near the mango.
I'll try that tomorrow.
Press it gently each day. When it feels slightly soft and smells sweet near the stalk, it's ready.
It's day three and a bit soft near the stalk. Is it ready?
If it smells sweet near the stalk, it's ready. Eat it soon, or put it in the fridge to slow the ripening.
Next week is a cousin's wedding in another city and I have to take a train alone for the first time.
That's a big step. Do you have your ticket and the train details ready?
Yes, the ticket's on my phone.
Keep a screenshot too, in case the signal is weak. Reach the station early, check the platform number on the board and sit near other families if you can.
What if I miss my stop?
Set an alarm for about twenty minutes before arrival, and check the station name on the boards when the train stops. You can also ask a fellow passenger or the ticket staff.
Will my parents call me during the journey?
Tell them you'll send a message at each big stop. That keeps everyone calm, including you.
Good idea. I'll share my seat number with them too.
Yes, and enjoy the window seat if you have one.
I was asked to fill in for a colleague next week, and I don't know all her tasks.
That's a fair thing to feel unsure about. Can you ask her for a handover list before she leaves?
She's already on leave.
Then ask your manager for the main tasks and who to contact when something is unclear. Make a list and tick items off.
Should I tell my manager that I'm unsure?
Yes, plainly and calmly. For example, 'I'd like to do this well. Could you tell me which tasks are most urgent?' That's professional and clear.
My manager says the tasks are on a shared sheet and I can't make sense of it.
Ask your manager or a teammate to walk you through it for ten minutes. Note which columns matter, and ask what each colour means.
Colour-coded, of course. I'll ask someone.
Sensible. Write the key on a sticky note so you remember it.
It's my first Karwa Chauth as a married woman. I'm nervous about doing everything right.
That's a lovely occasion, and it's normal to feel nervous at first. Is your mother-in-law or an elder family member guiding you?
Yes, she's been kind about it.
Then follow her lead and ask about anything you're unsure of. Families are usually glad to explain their way of doing things.
She said it's fine if I'm not perfect.
That's reassuring. The day is about the warmth, not about getting every step right.
My cricket bat feels too heavy. I swing late and get out early.
A heavy bat can slow your swing. Is it the right size for your height?
I got it from my cousin, who's taller.
That could be the reason. A bat that's too big is hard to control. Ask your coach to check whether the size and weight suit you.
Can I use it until I find another?
Yes, but practise with a lighter grip and shorter backlift to keep your timing. A bat that fits you will make a real difference.
I'll ask my coach on Saturday.
Perfect. Take the bat with you, so he can see it.
Is it true that the sun is a star? That sounds strange when it's so big and bright.
Yes, it's true. The sun is a star, and the stars you see at night are other suns that are very far away, which is why they look tiny.
How far is the sun, then?
Very far, but much closer than any other star. Its light takes about eight minutes to reach us, while light from the next nearest star takes over four years.
Wow. That makes me feel small.
It can, but it's also exciting to be part of such a big universe.
I loved the first half of my book and hated the ending. Is it okay to feel that way?
Of course. Readers often disagree with endings, even famous ones. What didn't you like?
Everything got solved too quickly.
That's a fair point. A rushed ending can feel less satisfying after a slow, careful start. You could imagine your own ending, or write a short version of how it could have gone.
Write my own ending, that sounds fun.
Try a page, keeping the same characters. It's a good writing exercise, and nobody needs to see it unless you want to share.
I want to say sorry to my brother after a fight, but I don't know how to start.
A simple start is best. You could say, 'I'm sorry about what I said. I didn't mean to hurt you.'
What if he ignores me?
Give him time. Some people need a little while before they're ready to talk. You've done your part by saying it.
Should I write it instead?
If speaking feels hard, a short note is fine. Slip it under his door or leave it on his desk, and keep it kind and short.
I left the note. He hasn't said anything.
That's all right. He has probably read it and may need time. Keep your day normal and be friendly when you see him.
What if he's still angry tomorrow?
Then give it another day. If a few days pass, a simple 'Want to watch something together?' reopens things without a big talk.
Our cat brought a dead lizard to the doorstep today. Why would she do that?
Cats are natural hunters, and bringing prey home is a common instinct. Some people think it's a gift, others think the cat is just storing her catch somewhere safe.
Should I scold her?
No, she won't understand, and it won't stop the instinct. Clear it up with gloves or a bag, wash your hands well, and try keeping her indoors at dawn and dusk when she hunts most.
I tried knitting a scarf and it's become a triangle somehow.
Ha, a very common stitch problem. A triangle usually means you're adding a stitch each row, often by accidentally looping the yarn at the edge.
How do I stop that?
Count the stitches at the end of each row, and check that you don't make an extra loop over the needle at the start of a row. A friend or an online tutorial can show you the edge stitch.
Maybe I'll turn the triangle into a bandana.
That's a smart rescue. Small triangles make nice neck scarves, and you'll get more practice with the next one.
Our bathroom door sticks in the monsoon and I have to push hard to open it.
Wood swells when the air is damp, so doors get tight in the rainy season. It's normal. Does the door rub on the frame?
Yes, near the top.
You can rub a candle or a bar of dry soap along the edge where it sticks, which lets it slide more easily. Ask an adult if the rubbing is serious, because a carpenter may need to plane it.
I'll try the soap.
A thin layer is enough. If the door shrinks back after the rains, you probably won't need more.
I read that the monsoon has reached our state early this year. Is that good?
Hmm, it depends. An early monsoon can bring welcome relief from the heat, and farmers might plant sooner. But it can also bring heavy rain before people are ready.
We aren't ready. Our terrace has leaks.
Then it's worth checking them now. Ask your parents or the building committee to look at the drains and patch any cracks before the heavy rain.
I'll tell my dad tonight.
A short chat now may save you a lot of buckets later.
I want to write a song for my sister's birthday but I don't know how to start.
That's a thoughtful gift. Start by writing a few lines about things you both enjoy or remember together. Does she have a favourite song?
She likes a slow, gentle one.
Then try using that same gentle mood. Write four short lines, make them rhyme in pairs and hum a simple tune that fits. It doesn't need to be fancy.
Do I need to be a singer?
Not at all. A song sung with care means more than a perfect voice. You can even read the words aloud like a poem if you prefer.
I wrote four lines, but one doesn't rhyme. Is that a problem?
Not at all. Songs don't need perfect rhymes. If it flows when you sing it, it works. You can also change a word to make it fit.
I'll change 'bright' to 'light'.
That's a neat swap. Read all four lines aloud once to hear how they sound.
I've been told to use different passwords for each account, but I can't remember them all.
That's good advice, but it's hard to remember many. A password manager built into your device is one safe tool, and a family member can help you set it up.
Is writing them in a notebook okay?
At home, a notebook kept in a safe place is better than reusing one weak password everywhere. Don't write the account name next to the password in an obvious way, and don't carry it around.
I'll try the notebook at home first.
Fine, and make each password long. A short sentence with a few odd words is easier to remember than random letters.
My friend wants me to skip a lecture to hang out, and I have an attendance problem already.
It sounds tempting, but with your attendance in mind, skipping might cause trouble. Can you meet her after class instead?
She says it'll only be this once.
You can tell her honestly, 'I can't risk my attendance, but I'd love to meet at four.' A real friend will understand, and you still get your time together.
That's fair. I'll suggest the later time.
That keeps both your attendance and the plan safe. Enjoy the afternoon.
The shop is giving a free pen with every notebook, and I'm tempted to buy more notebooks than I need.
That's the sort of offer designed to tempt. How many notebooks do you actually need this term?
Maybe four. The offer is for six.
Then buy the four. A free pen isn't a bargain if you spend on notebooks you won't use. If your friends need some, you could split the offer with them.
Splitting is clever. My friend needs two.
Then you both get what you need and a pen each. Everyone wins.
My friend wants to pay me back for her two notebooks later. Should I remind her?
A friendly mention is fine. Say, 'Whenever you're ready, the notebooks were this much.' Keep it light so it doesn't feel like pressure.
I'll tell her at lunch.
Sounds good. Most friends appreciate a clear, kind reminder.
Our lane has a lot of dogs, and some neighbours are afraid of them. How do we keep everyone comfortable?
It's a fair concern from both sides. Dog owners can keep their dogs on leashes in shared spaces and clean up after them.
What about people who are very scared?
They can be given space. Owners can hold the leash short when passing, and a friendly 'hello, we'll go slowly' helps too. A small lane meeting to agree on a few simple rules often calms everyone.
I forgot the lines for our class play in the middle of the scene and the whole room went silent.
That's a tough moment, and it happens to nearly every actor. How did you recover?
Another girl whispered my line.
That's what a cast is for. Next time, practise the scene with a friend who can give you the first words of each line, and keep a small card backstage if your teacher allows it.
Everyone laughed afterwards. I wanted to crawl under the stage.
Most of them were probably laughing with relief that it wasn't them. If someone brings it up, smile and say, 'That was my dramatic pause.'
Ha, I like that.
Using humour is a nice way to move on. And you'll remember your lines better next time.
My uncle says he'll teach me to drive when I turn eighteen, and I'm already nervous.
It's a good way to learn, with someone patient beside you. You still have time before that. What worries you most?
Other vehicles on the road.
That's why learners usually start in an empty place, such as a quiet ground, and move to roads only when they feel steady. A registered driving instructor can also help.
Do I need to learn rules first?
Yes, rules come first. Reading the road signs and the rules from the official handbook will make the practice easier, and your uncle can quiz you.
That sounds good. I'll start with the handbook.
A good plan, and you'll have time to learn at an easy pace.
My friend asked if she could bring her cousin along to our weekend movie. I'm not sure how I feel.
It's okay to have mixed feelings. Do you know her cousin?
Not really.
Then it might be a nice chance to meet someone new. You could say, 'Sure, bring her. We'll make space.' If you still feel unsure, tell your friend openly that you were hoping for a small group.
I think I'll say yes. It's just a movie.
That's a relaxed way to look at it, and a new face might become a new friend.
My cake came out brown on top but still wet in the middle. What did I do wrong?
That usually means the oven was too hot, so the top cooked before the middle could set. Next time, lower the temperature a little and bake for longer.
Can I save this one?
Yes. Cover the top loosely with foil and put it back in the oven for ten minutes at a lower heat. Check with a clean toothpick, which should come out dry.
Our flight leaves early in the morning and I'm worried I'll oversleep.
Set two alarms at different times, and put one phone across the room so you have to get up. Pack your bag and keep your documents by the door the night before.
What if both alarms fail?
Ask a family member to wake you as a backup, and sleep a little earlier than usual. A calm last evening makes the morning smoother.
I have to write a thank-you note to a client who gave us a big order. How formal should it be?
Polite and warm, but short. Start with the name, say thank you for the order, add one line about looking forward to working together and sign off with your name.
Should I mention the project by name?
Yes, a brief mention shows you remember the details. Something like, 'Thank you for choosing us for the school project' is friendly and clear.
Our family makes a rice kolam outside the door on Pongal, but this year I'm in charge and I've never done one.
A rice kolam is a lovely job to take on. Start with a simple pattern, like a row of dots joined by curves. Do you have a small design in mind?
I'd like a flower shape.

A flower works well. Make a grid of dots, say five by five, then join them with curved lines to form petals. Practise it on paper first and then pinch the rice flour between your fingers to draw it on the floor.
I just got roller skates and I can't stop without crashing into the wall.
That's the usual first problem. Practise in an open area, with no traffic or walls nearby. Do you have a helmet and pads for your knees and wrists?
Yes, I wear them.
Good. To slow down, try to bend your knees slightly and glide with feet parallel, then press the brake pad on the heel of one skate gently. Practise this at a slow speed first.
A tiny plant is growing out of a crack in the pavement. How does it even survive?
Seeds get blown or dropped into cracks, where a little soil and rainwater gather. The crack holds moisture and protects the seedling from being trampled.
Should I leave it?
Yes, as long as it isn't in anyone's way. It's a nice reminder of how tough plants can be. If it blocks a path, you could move it to a pot.
I peek at the last page of books before I finish them. Is that cheating?
Not at all. Plenty of readers do it, because knowing the ending helps them relax and enjoy the journey. It's your book.
But my friends say it ruins the story.
For some people it does, and for others it doesn't. Try it both ways with different books and see which feels better to you.
My viva is next Tuesday and I freeze when teachers ask me questions face to face.
A viva makes many students nervous. Do you know which topics they'll ask about?
The project I submitted, mostly.
Then you already have an advantage. Read your own report twice, and for each section, say aloud what you did and why. Ask a friend to play the examiner.
What if I don't know an answer?
Say so calmly, then explain what you do know. Something like, 'I'm not sure about that detail, but here is what I found.' Examiners usually respect honesty more than guessing.
I'll practise with my roommate tonight.
Practise standing up and speaking clearly, as you will in the room. It helps your voice settle.
It's tomorrow. How do I calm down in the morning?
Eat a light breakfast, go over your key points once and then stop studying. Arrive early, take a few slow breaths outside the room and remember that examiners want to hear what you know.
I forgot my lab coat and the lab starts in ten minutes.
Ask a classmate who has a spare, or check if your lab assistant keeps extra coats. Is anyone from your batch nearby?
Yes, my friend Isha is in the corridor.
Ask her quickly, and offer to return it right after class. If she has none, speak to the lab assistant before the session, rather than waiting for someone to notice.
I wanted to take a front seat in lectures but my friends always grab the last row.
Ha, the last row has a loyal fan club. Why do you prefer the front?
I can hear better and I don't get distracted.
That's a good reason. You could politely say, 'I'll sit at the front, can we meet after class?' Friends usually don't mind.
Won't it look odd if I sit alone?
It might feel odd on the first day. Often one or two others join once they see the front is the sensible spot, and teachers tend to remember attentive students.
I'll try it next Monday.
Good luck. At worst, you'll have the best view and clear notes.
It worked. Two others joined me in the front today.
Ha, you started a trend. Front-row people unite. Enjoy the clear notes.
Our colony's group chat is full of 'good morning' pictures and I can't find the important notices anymore.
That's a common chat problem. Is there an admin who manages the group?
Yes, our secretary.
You could ask him to pin important notices, or suggest creating a separate group just for announcements. Say it politely, such as, 'Could we keep one group only for notices?'
Will people be offended?
Most won't, especially if you say that the greetings are lovely but get in the way. A calm, general request works better than naming anyone.
Okay, I'll message him now.
Sounds good. Keep it short and friendly.
He pinned a notice and made a separate announcements group. People are joining.
That's a quick result. Your polite request helped, and now notices are easy to find. A small thank-you to him would be nice.
A street light near our lane has been off for two weeks and it's very dark at night.
That could be unsafe for people walking. Has anyone reported it?
Not sure. Everyone assumes someone else did.
Then it's worth checking. Your local municipal office or ward office usually has a complaint line or an online form. Note the pole number if there is one, and the exact spot.
Should I ask neighbours to sign something?
A joint complaint can carry weight, but even one clear complaint works. Ask your resident group if they can follow up so it doesn't get forgotten.
We want to hold a potluck on our terrace for Diwali, but I'm worried about the planning.
A potluck is easy to organise if you keep it simple. Roughly how many families are coming?
About ten.
Make a shared list where each family writes the dish they will bring, so you don't end up with ten desserts. Add a few categories like starters, mains, sweets and drinks.
Who brings plates?
Ask one family to take care of plates and napkins, and another to look after the lights and seating. Splitting small jobs keeps it relaxed.
I'll make a chart on a chart paper and stick it near the lift.
That's visible and friendly. A deadline for filling in the chart will help too.
Eight families have already filled in the chart. Four are bringing sweets!
Time to nudge a few towards mains. Add a note under the chart saying, 'We need two more main dishes and one salad,' and people will adjust.
My friend got a brand new bicycle and I felt jealous. Then I felt bad about feeling jealous.
That's very human. Feeling jealous doesn't make you a bad person, it just means you wanted something. What do you like about the bicycle?
It's red, and it has gears.
So you really like it. You could let the feeling pass and still be happy for your friend. Maybe ask for a short ride, and think about whether you could save up for one someday.
It's Sunday evening and I feel a heavy kind of sadness. School starts tomorrow.
Sunday evening blues are very common. Is there something about tomorrow that worries you, or is it just the end of the weekend?
Mostly the weekend ending. But there's a maths test too.
Then it might be a mix. Write down what you'll need for the test and do a short revision now, so you wake up feeling more prepared. After that, do something calm you enjoy, like music or a walk.
I giggled when the teacher dropped her chalk and now I feel awful about it.
It's natural to laugh at surprises, especially when everyone is quiet. Did she notice you?
I think so. She looked at me.
Then a quick, sincere word could help. After class, you could say, 'I'm sorry I laughed earlier. It was the surprise.' Most teachers appreciate that.
What if she's already forgotten?
Then it costs you nothing and she may smile. And you'll feel lighter.
I tried folding a paper crane from a video, but mine looks like a sad pigeon.
Ha, the first crane is often a pigeon. Which step goes wrong?
The wings. They won't open properly.
Wing folds depend on sharp creases. Press each fold flat with your fingernail, and make sure the paper is square. Thin paper is easier than thick.
I only have notebook paper.
That's fine for practice. Cut a square from a page and use it. After a few tries, the folds will get cleaner, and you'll have a flock of pigeons first and then cranes.
I've been drawing faces and the eyes always look uneven.
That's a common challenge. A trick is to remember that the eyes sit roughly halfway down the head, with about one eye-width of space between them.
I put them too high, I think.
Many beginners do. Draw a light oval, mark a line across the middle and place the eyes on that line. Rub out the guidelines when you're done.
Do I need a model?
A mirror or a photo helps a lot. Try looking at your own face or a family photo, and draw what you see rather than what you think a face looks like.
I'll try the mirror tonight.
Fun. Pull a funny face and draw that too, for the practice.
I drew my own face with the mirror. The nose is huge.
Ha, noses are the hardest part. Look at the shadows under the nose rather than its outline, and draw with light lines first. Rub out and adjust, and it will shrink to size.
I've been trying to whistle for a week and I only get air.
That's how everyone starts. Wet your lips, shape them into a small circle and blow gently, like you're cooling hot tea.
I do that, but it's just a hiss.
Then adjust a little. Make the circle smaller and move your tongue a bit back. Experiment until you hear a faint note, then hold it steady.
The tap in our kitchen drips all night and I can hear it from my room.
A drip is annoying and it wastes water. Does it stop when you tighten the handle fully?
No, it keeps dripping.
Then the washer inside may be worn. That's a small job for a plumber or an adult who knows how to do it. Meanwhile, put a cloth or a small bowl under the tap to muffle the sound.
Can I tell my parents?
Yes, ask them to call someone. A quick fix now saves water and your sleep.
My sister and I share a cupboard and she keeps mixing our clothes.
That can be irritating. Have you tried splitting the cupboard into sections?
Not really. She just puts things anywhere.
Try dividing it into two halves, perhaps with a ribbon or labels. You could ask her which side she wants, so she has a say in it.
What if she still mixes them?
Remind her calmly, and put her clothes back without fuss. Over a few weeks, the habit often settles.
I want to move my study table next to the window, but my mom thinks it will be too bright.
Natural light is great for studying, and mid-day glare can bother the eyes. Which way does the window face?
East. So it's bright in the morning.
Then the table can work well, since morning light is gentle. A thin curtain can soften it if it ever gets too strong. Keep the screen or book at an angle, so the light doesn't glare on it.
I want to learn to read sheet music, but the notes look like a secret code.
It's a code, but a friendly one. Start with the lines and spaces on the staff, and learn the names of the notes in order.
How long does that take?
A week of ten-minute practice sessions can teach you the basics. Use an easy rhyme to remember them, and try reading very simple tunes first.
Should I learn the notes or the rhythm first?
Both matter, but start by clapping simple rhythms so the beat becomes natural. Then add the notes, one or two at a time.
A song has been stuck in my head all day and it's driving me mad.
Ha, that's called an earworm. Do you know the whole song, or only one line?
Just the chorus, over and over.
Try listening to the full song once, since your brain often wants to hear the ending. Then listen to something different, or chew gum, or talk to someone.
Why does it get stuck?
Repetitive, catchy tunes tend to play on a loop in the mind, and not finishing the tune can keep the loop going. Finishing it or switching activities usually breaks it.
I'll finish the song then. Hopefully it leaves.
If it doesn't, try humming something different. Your brain may take the hint.
It left for ten minutes and then a different song arrived.
You have a full playlist in your head. Keep busy with something that needs thinking, like a puzzle, and the tunes tend to fade.
Our school talent show is next week and I can't choose between singing and playing the flute.
Both sound lovely. Which one do you feel more confident doing in front of people?
Singing. But the flute is more unusual.
Being confident usually matters more than being unusual. If singing makes you comfortable, you'll perform better. You could also play a short flute piece between two verses if the time allows.
Our puppy chewed my slipper today. I'm not sure whether to scold him.
Puppies chew things because they're teething and curious. Scolding after the fact usually doesn't work, because he won't connect it with the chewing.
What should I do?
Keep slippers out of reach and give him a safe chew toy. If you catch him chewing something wrong, say 'no' calmly and swap it for the toy.
Hopefully he learns soon.
He will, with patience. Praise him when he chews the toy, and he'll learn what's allowed.
My budgie sleeps with his head tucked in his feathers. Is something wrong?
That's normal. Many birds sleep with their head turned back and tucked under a wing. It keeps them warm and comfortable.
Okay. I was worried.
It's kind of you to notice. If he seems sleepy all day, puffed up or stops eating, ask a vet who treats birds. Otherwise, sleeping like this is part of his routine.
I'm looking after my neighbour's rabbit for a week. I've never had a rabbit.
That's a nice job. Did your neighbour leave instructions about food and the cage?
A list, yes. Hay, some vegetables and fresh water.
Then follow the list closely and keep the water fresh. Rabbits like routine, so feed him at the same times each day.
What if he seems lonely?
Spend a bit of quiet time near him, talk softly and let him come to you. Don't pick him up too much, as rabbits can be nervous.
Can I let him run around the room?
Only if your neighbour said it's fine, and only in a safe, closed room with wires and small objects out of reach. If you aren't sure, ask them before doing it.
Your advice worked. He nibbled a carrot from my hand today.
That's a trust milestone. Keep your hand still and let him come to you, and give treats only as your neighbour allows.
The shop says everything is half price today, and I'm tempted to buy things I don't need.
A sale can make anything look useful. What did you go in to buy?
A school bag. But there are nice pencil cases too.
Buy the bag, and ask yourself whether you'd buy the pencil case at full price. If not, it can wait. Sales come back, and you will still have a bag.
I'm ordering a birthday cake for my dad. How do I choose the right flavour?
Think about what he usually enjoys. Does he like chocolate, fruit or something plain?
He likes pineapple cake.
Then pineapple is a lovely choice. Call the bakery a day or two ahead to confirm the flavour, size and the time you want to collect it.
Should I ask them to write something?
Yes, keep the message short, such as 'Happy Birthday, Dad.' If the bakery does names, spell it clearly over the phone and repeat it back to check.
I'll tell them at the counter, so I can see how it's written.
That's a smart way to avoid mistakes.
I want to buy a raincoat, but I'm not sure whether to get a long one or a short one.
Both have uses. A long raincoat covers more of you but can be heavy to walk in, while a short one is lighter. How do you travel?
By bicycle, mostly.
For a bicycle, a short one is easier to move in, and a long one could catch in the wheel. Look for bright colours or reflective strips to stay visible in the rain.
The Wi-Fi in my room is so slow that videos keep buffering.
That's frustrating. Where is the router compared with your room?
It's in the hall, two walls away.
Walls weaken the signal. Try moving closer to the router, or ask an adult if the router can be placed in a more central spot. Also check whether many devices are using it at once.
My brother is always downloading something.
That can slow everyone's connection. You could agree on times, so downloads happen when you aren't studying or watching something.
I'll talk to him tonight.
A friendly schedule is easier than an argument.
A number I don't know keeps calling me and I'm nervous about picking up.
It's wise to be careful. You don't have to answer unknown numbers. Have you told your parents?
Not yet.
Tell them, so they can decide what to do. If it keeps happening, they can block the number, and you can avoid sharing any personal details on a call you didn't expect.
What if it's something important?
Important callers usually leave a message or try again. If you want, ask an adult to call the number back with you nearby.
I want to edit a short video of my trip, but I've never done it before.
Sounds fun. Do you have an editing app on your phone?
Yes, it came with it.
Start by choosing your best clips and trimming each to a few seconds. Put them in order, add a simple title and a soft music track, and keep the whole video short.
How long should the video be?
About one to two minutes is nice for a trip. Shorter videos are easier to finish, and people enjoy watching them to the end.
I'll try it this evening.
Save your project often, so you don't lose your work if the phone shuts down.
I finished it. How do I share it with my family?
Export it to your phone's gallery, then send it through a chat or share a link. If the file is big, a family member can copy it onto a pen drive.
The summer holidays are here and it's too hot to play outside in the afternoon.
That's a common problem. Mornings and evenings are better for outdoor play. What do you like to do?
Cricket, mostly. But the heat is unbearable at noon.
Then play early in the morning or after the sun goes down. In the afternoon, you can try indoor games, drawing or reading. Keep a bottle of water close.
There's a loud thunderstorm and I can't sleep. The flashes are bright.
Storms can be noisy and startling. Are you inside, in your bed?
Yes, under the blanket.

That's a safe place. Try closing the curtains to block the flashes, and play soft music or a fan to cover the noise. Count slowly between the flash and the thunder, and you'll notice the gap getting bigger as the storm moves away.
Why does that happen?
Light travels almost instantly, while sound travels more slowly. A longer gap means the lightning is farther away.
We haven't had rain for weeks and my balcony plants look so dry.
Dry spells are hard on plants. Are you watering them daily?
Every evening, but they still droop in the afternoon.
The afternoon sun may be drying them quickly. Try watering early in the morning as well, and moving the pots to a spot with afternoon shade. A layer of dry leaves on the soil helps hold moisture.
Dry leaves from where?
From the ground downstairs, or any garden or tree you can sweep. A thin layer is enough, so the soil can still breathe.
I'll try the leaves tomorrow.
Great. Check the soil with a finger to see if it's damp below the surface.
Rain came last night and the plants look happier!
What a relief. Don't water them today, since the soil is already damp. Pick off any dead leaves and enjoy the fresh air.
I'm gifting a poetry book to my friend, but I've never bought one. How do I choose?
Think about her mood and taste. Does she like funny verses, nature poems or love poems?
Nature, I think. She loves hiking.
Then a collection of nature poems or poems about travel would suit her. Look at the first few pages in the shop, to see if the language is easy and enjoyable.
Should I add a note?
A short note is a lovely touch. You could mark a poem you like with a bookmark and write a line about it.
My little sister and I play a dictionary game where we pick a random word and guess its meaning. Any ideas to make it better?
That's a fun game. You could add points for the closest guess, or each write a sentence using the word after you find the real meaning.
Do you think it helps with learning?
Yes, guessing makes you notice the word, and you'll remember it better when you check. Writing a sentence makes it stick even more.
We could keep a scoreboard.
Yes, a scoreboard on the fridge. Keep a list of the words you learned, and you'll be surprised by how many you collect.
A funny trophy for the winner too.
Why not? A paper crown for the Word Champion could be a hit.
She picked 'Word Champion' as the prize. Her first word was 'tintinnabulation'.
Wow, a dramatic start. Look it up together, then both try using it in a sentence. A hard word makes a fun first round.
I found my grandfather's old photo album, and I don't know who most of the people are.
What a treasure. Is your grandfather around to tell you about them?
He is, but he's a bit forgetful now.
Then go through the album together, a few photos at a time. Don't press him if he can't recall names. Write down what he does remember on small notes next to the photos.
What if he gets upset?
Let it be relaxed, like a chat. If he seems tired or confused, put the album away and try again another day. The stories he does tell are the best part.
My brother and I both want to use the study room at the same time every evening.
It sounds like you need a schedule. Do you each have different study needs, such as quiet versus music?
He studies with music, and I need silence.
Then try splitting the room by time. One of you uses it first with the door closed, and the other uses the living room or another quiet corner. Swap each week.
What if he doesn't agree?
Suggest a trial week, and say you can change it if it doesn't work. People often agree to something temporary. Ask a parent to help set the schedule if you can't agree.
We want to take part in Janmashtami's dahi handi at our colony, but my mom is worried about safety.
Her worry makes sense, because human pyramids can be risky. What role did you have in mind?
I'd be on the ground, helping to hold the rope.
Ground helpers matter a lot. Show your mother how the organisers plan safety, such as soft mats, a helmet for the top person and adults standing by.
What if they don't have any of that?
Then it's reasonable to sit this one out and enjoy the celebration as a spectator. You could help with decorations or the prasad instead, and your mom will feel better.
Our gurdwara is asking for young volunteers to serve langar this Guru Nanak Jayanti, and I've never done it.
That's a meaningful way to take part. Do you know what the volunteers usually do?
I think they serve food and clean up.
Yes, plus helping to lay out mats and wash utensils. Ask the organisers what you should wear and how early to come. Wash your hands, tie your hair back and cover your head as they request.
Is there anything I should avoid doing?
Follow the instructions of the senior volunteers, and don't rush or wander off. If you aren't sure about something, ask politely.
My coconut chutney came out too watery. Can I fix it?
Yes. Add a spoonful of roasted gram, known as pottukadalai, or a little more grated coconut, and blend again briefly. They thicken it without changing the taste much.
I don't have roasted gram.
Then try a small piece of bread soaked and squeezed dry, or just a little more coconut. If you have none, serve it as a dip for dosa, since a thinner chutney works too.
It's my first time cooking pasta and I'm afraid it'll stick together.
Use a large pot with plenty of boiling, salted water, and stir during the first minute or two. Does your pasta packet have instructions?
Yes, it says ten minutes.
Follow that, but taste a piece at nine minutes. When it's soft with a little bite, drain it and rinse with warm water if you're not adding sauce at once.
What if it still sticks?
Toss it with a spoon of oil. Next time, stir more at the start and keep the water bubbling.
I'll report back with pasta pictures.
I'd love to hear how it turned out. Good luck.
We're doing a secret gift exchange in our friend group and I got the name of someone I barely know.
That's a fun challenge. Do you know anything about her?
She likes drawing, I think.
Then a small sketchbook, a set of colour pencils or a nice eraser would be a lovely gift. You could ask a mutual friend for hints without giving away that you're her gifter.
What if she doesn't like it?
Most people appreciate the thought, especially when it matches their interest. Keep it small and useful, and include a kind note.
My friend forgot my birthday and I'm a bit hurt. I don't want to make a big deal.
It's okay to feel hurt, even if you don't show it. Was it a busy time for her?
She has exams.
Then she may have simply lost track of the date. You could mention it gently later, like, 'I missed hearing from you on my birthday, but I know exams are hard.' That's honest and kind.
I'd rather joke about it.
That works too. You could say, 'You owe me a cake.' Laughing about it can ease things and she'll likely make it up to you.
There's a long line of ants going up our wall every morning. Where are they going?
They're probably following a scent trail to a food source. Worker ants leave a chemical track, and others follow it to bring food back to the nest.
How do they find it?
One ant finds the food, then returns to the nest leaving a trail. Others follow it, add to the trail and strengthen it. If there's no food left, the trail fades.
So I should check for crumbs.
Yes. Wipe the area and store sweets in closed boxes, and the ants will move on.
Why does the moon look different every night?
The moon doesn't make its own light. We see the part that the sun lights, and as the moon travels around the Earth, we see different amounts of that lit side.
So it's not changing shape?
No, it stays round. What changes is how much of the lit half faces us. Full moon means we see all of it, and new moon means almost none.
I volunteered for our school's science exhibition, but I don't know what jobs I can do.
There's usually a lot to do. You could help set up tables, guide visitors or explain a model. Which one sounds fun?
Guiding visitors, I guess.
Then learn the main points of a few projects, so you can tell people briefly what each shows. Practise a simple opening, such as, 'Hello, this one shows how...'
What if they ask hard questions?
Say, 'Good question, let me check with the student who made it.' Nobody expects you to know everything.
That's a relief.
Wear your name tag, smile and enjoy meeting visitors.
It went well. A visitor asked something I couldn't answer.
That happens even to experts. You did the right thing if you said you'd check. Note the question and find the answer with the project student afterwards.
Parent-teacher meeting is next week and I'm scared my teacher will say something bad about me.
That feeling is common. Teachers often share both strengths and things to improve. What worries you most?
That I talk too much in class.
If that's true, it's better to hear it so that you can work on it. You could tell your parents beforehand and say you're trying to do better.
Won't they be upset?
Perhaps a little, but they'll likely appreciate your honesty. It shows maturity.
I'm learning table tennis and my serve keeps going into the net.
That's a common issue. Are you tossing the ball up before you hit it?
Sometimes I forget.
Toss the ball straight up, hold your racket open and hit it so it bounces on your side first, then crosses the net. Practise on a table with a small target on your side.
How do I get more control?
Short, slow serves help you build control. Speed comes later. Practise ten serves at a time and count how many you land correctly.
I'll aim for six in ten this week.
A clear goal like that is helpful, and it will improve your focus.
Our school is organising a walkathon and I'm a slow walker.
That's fine. A walkathon is about taking part, not winning. How long is the route?
A few kilometres.
Wear comfortable shoes, carry water and set a steady pace you can keep. If you walk with a friend, you can talk along the way and the distance feels shorter.
What if I fall behind the group?
There are usually volunteers along the way. Keep going at your own pace, and you'll finish when you finish.
We're visiting my grandparents' village for a week and there's hardly any mobile signal. I'm already worried.
That could actually be a nice break. Is there a landline or somewhere you can get signal for urgent calls?
There's a spot near the temple where it works.
Then tell your friends you'll be offline mostly and check there once a day. Bring a book, cards or a sketchpad for downtime.
What will I do all day?
Explore, help your grandparents with small jobs, listen to their stories and notice the quiet. You might find you enjoy it more than you expect.
I'm travelling on a bus with my little brother, who is four. How do I keep him calm?
Short journeys are easy, longer ones need a plan. How long is the trip?
About three hours.
Pack a few small things: a picture book, a snack, a bottle of water and a favourite toy. Point out things outside the window and play simple games like finding red objects.
What if he needs the toilet?
Ask the conductor or driver about the next stop and keep him close at the stop. It's helpful to take him just before boarding as well.
Okay. I'll pack some biscuits for him.
That should keep him happy. Bring wet wipes too, for sticky fingers.
I wrote an email to my manager and now I think it sounds rude. How do I check the tone?
Read it aloud, and imagine receiving it yourself. Does it sound friendly and clear?
It sounds a bit blunt.
Add a greeting, a 'please' where you're asking for something and a short thank-you at the end. Replace commands with polite requests, like 'Could you please send...'
Will that make it too long?
Not if you stay brief. Two or three extra words change the tone a lot, and the message stays short.
I'm working remotely for the first time and I struggle to stay on track at home.
That's an adjustment. Do you have a dedicated space to work?
Just my bed.
Try setting up a table or a corner just for work, even a small one. It helps your mind separate work from rest. Keep regular hours and take breaks.
What should my breaks be like?
Stretch, drink water, step outside for a few minutes or call a friend. Avoid starting something that will take you away for an hour, like a long show.
Okay. I'll put a small table by the window.
Natural light helps. A tidy desk and a closed laptop at the end of the day will make the work feel finished.
A week in, and it's going better. But I miss chatting with colleagues.
That's normal. Set up a short video chat once or twice a week, or take a virtual coffee break with a teammate. A few minutes of casual talk brings back the office feeling.
I missed my usual bus and I have an exam in forty minutes.
Stay calm and think about the quickest option. Is there another bus, an auto or a metro you can take?
An auto, but it will cost more than I planned.
Then take it. An exam matters more than a bit of extra fare, and being on time keeps you calm. Ask the driver for the fastest route, and keep your admit card ready.
I found one. Do I tell the invigilator I'm late if I arrive just in time?
Only if you actually arrive after the start. If you walk in on time, just find your seat. Take two deep breaths before you open the paper.
I'm in the auto now. Thanks.
Sit back and keep your hall ticket in your hand. You've prepared for this, and the ride is the hard part done.
I made it with ten minutes to spare.
Excellent. Use the extra minutes to sit down and breathe, then read the instructions on the paper slowly before you start writing.
I've been asked to give a short farewell speech for the seniors. I don't know what to say.
What an honour. A farewell speech works best when it's short and warm. Is there a memory you share with the seniors?
They helped us a lot during orientation.
Start there. Thank them for the help, mention one funny or kind moment and wish them luck. Two minutes is plenty.
My professor speaks quickly and has an accent I find hard to follow, so my notes are a mess.
That's a common challenge. Does the professor share slides or a reading list?
Slides, yes, after class.
Then use the slides to fill gaps. Leave space in your notes, write down key words as you hear them and match them to the slides afterwards. You can also ask a classmate to compare notes.
Should I ask the professor to slow down?
You can, politely. Something like, 'Could you repeat that last point, please?' Most professors are glad when students ask, and others in the class will likely be thankful too.
I'll try it tomorrow.
Prepare a question or two beforehand and you'll feel more confident.
I asked him to repeat a point and he did, with a smile.
That's a good sign. Professors usually appreciate attentive students. Keep your questions short and you'll soon get used to his pace.
A neighbour keeps asking to borrow our ladder and I don't always want to lend it.
It's fine to have limits with your belongings. Is it a problem because the ladder doesn't come back, or because you need it?
Mostly because it comes back late and dusty.
Then you could say, 'Please bring it back by evening and wipe it down.' If it still bothers you, suggest they get their own, or share the cost of one with others in the lane.
I don't want to sound rude.
A friendly tone and a clear request are not rude. People generally respect a polite 'Yes, as long as...'
I'll say that next time.
Short and kind is all it needs.
He said sure, and he even wiped it. Maybe I overthought it.
That happens a lot. A clear sentence often settles a worry that grew bigger in your head.
Our community hall is hosting a children's drawing competition and I've been asked to help.
That sounds fun. What can you take care of?
Probably setting up the tables and handing out sheets.
Good, those tasks matter. Make sure each child has enough space, and keep extra pencils and erasers in a box. Ask the organisers about a time limit and a theme.
What if a child gets upset when the results are announced?
Have a small certificate or sticker for every participant, so nobody leaves empty-handed. And a kind word, like 'I loved your colours,' goes a long way.
We could also display all the drawings on a wall.
Great idea. Families love seeing the work, and it makes every child feel valued.
I'll suggest it to the organisers.
Do, and offer to help hang them up with tape that won't damage the wall.
Our building has started separating wet and dry waste, but some neighbours keep mixing it up.
That takes a while to become a habit. Does the building have clear labels on the bins?
Yes, but they're small.
Larger labels with pictures can help a lot. You could suggest a notice with simple examples, like peels and leftovers in the wet bin and paper and plastic in the dry one.
I start a new dance class tomorrow and I can't stop worrying that everyone will be better than me.
It's normal to feel that way before something new. Most people in a class have different levels. Is it a beginner class?
Yes, but some of them are bound to have learned before.
Maybe, and that's fine. The teacher knows beginners need time, and others will be busy thinking about their own steps. Focus on enjoying the music and learning one thing.
What if I forget the steps?
Watch the people in front, smile and carry on. Dancers laugh at their own mistakes all the time.
Will it help if I arrive early?
Yes, you can meet the teacher, find a spot in the room and settle in. Wear comfortable clothes.
I'll do that. Thanks for the pep talk.
Enjoy it. By the end of the first class, you might wish you'd started sooner.
I finished writing my first short story today and I feel proud. Is it okay to feel that?
Absolutely. Finishing something creative is an achievement, so a bit of pride is well earned.
I want to tell people but I'm afraid they'll laugh.
Start with someone kind, like a friend or family member who is gentle with feedback. Tell them you'd like honest but kind comments.
I get angry very fast, and then I say things I regret.
Many people struggle with that. Does it usually happen at home, at school, or everywhere?
Mostly at home, with my brother.
A pause can help. When you feel the anger rise, take a slow breath and count to ten before you speak. If you need to, step out of the room for a minute.
What if I'm too angry to stop?
Then walk away and say, 'I need a break.' That's not running away, it's protecting the conversation. Come back when you've calmed down.
And if I've already said something mean?
Apologise briefly and honestly, like, 'I'm sorry I said that. I was angry.' Then try the pause next time. If it keeps happening, a trusted adult or school counsellor can help.
My little cousin and I made paper boats and want to race them. Any ideas?
Fun. A tub, a bucket or a shallow stream would work as a race track. Do you have a safe place with water?
Our balcony tub, I think.
Perfect. Blow on the boats to move them, or use a straw. Draw a finish line on a card. For a sail, add a small triangle from paper.
Our boats are sinking quickly.
Paper soaks up water. Rub a candle over the surface, which makes it water-resistant, or use waxed paper for the boats. Fold carefully, so the hull stays tight.
A candle? Clever.
It works for a short race. Dry the boats on a towel afterwards, and you can race again.
The candle trick worked! Which boat will win?
That depends on your race. Try again with a taller or smaller sail and see which shape wins.
Planning a comic strip about a talking mango, but I'm no artist.
A talking mango sounds hilarious. Comics don't need great drawings. Simple shapes and clear faces are enough.
What if my drawings look childish?
Many popular comics use very simple drawings. The story and the jokes matter more. Use big speech bubbles and keep the text short.
How many panels should I draw?
Start with four. Panel one sets the scene, two adds a problem, three builds the joke and four gives the punchline.
Can you suggest a first joke?
You could have the mango say, 'I'm so ripe, I can't even peel myself together.' It's a pun, so adjust it to your style.
Ha, I'll use something like that.
Ha, I hope it makes you smile. Add a tiny face on the mango and the rest follows.
I collect seashells whenever we visit the beach. Now I have a big pile and no idea what to do with them.
That's a lovely collection. You could sort them by type or colour and display them in a glass jar or a shallow box.
They smell a bit fishy.
Wash them in warm soapy water and let them dry in the sun, so any smell goes away. If any still smells, leave it outdoors for a few days.
The fridge is full of random containers and I can't find anything.
A clean-out will help. Take everything out, check what's still good and wipe the shelves. Do you have a good spot for the things you use most?
Not really.
Put daily items like milk and curd at eye level, and keep leftovers in clear boxes at the front, so you notice them. Use one shelf for fruit and veg.
What about the door?
Use it for sauces and small bottles, since it's a bit warmer. Label containers with the date, and eat the oldest food first.
That sounds sensible. I'll do it on Sunday.
Put on some music while you do it. It turns a chore into something almost fun.
I cleaned it. I found a jar of something I can't identify.
Check the date and smell, and if you can't tell what it is, it's safest to throw it out. Wash the jar before you reuse it.
I'm arranging my bookshelf by colour, and my brother says that's silly.
It can look beautiful, and it's your shelf. Can you still find the books you want?
Sort of. I remember the covers.
Then it works for you. If you ever need a system, you could put textbooks on one shelf by subject and the colourful ones on another. Or just say, 'It's a rainbow, not a library.'
Ha, I'll tell him that.
And let him know he's welcome to borrow from the rainbow.
He actually said it looks cool. Now he wants his comics in the rainbow too.
That's the best outcome. Let him add them by spine colour, and you may end up with a shared rainbow.
I'd like to make a reading nook on our balcony. It's tiny.
A small space can be cosy. How wide is it?
Just big enough for a chair.
Then a chair with a cushion and a small stool for books and a drink would work. Hang a thin curtain or place a plant to give it some privacy.
What about the sun and rain?
A light curtain or a bamboo blind on the open side can help with the sun. For the rain, move the cushions inside, or keep a plastic cover handy.
I'll put up a small hook for the cushion.
Smart. A hook near the door means you can grab it quickly when the clouds roll in.
I can't wait to read there.
Choose a long, good book for the first evening, and keep a pair of woollen socks nearby for chilly nights.
We have to learn the recorder at school and I can't get any clear notes.
That's a common problem at the start. Are you covering the holes completely with the pads of your fingers?
I think so, but some air leaks.
Check that each finger sits flat on its hole, and blow gently, as if saying 'too' softly. Blowing hard makes a squeal.
Ah, that's what I was doing. Thanks!
Squeals are no fun for anyone, so you've fixed it. Practise a few soft notes each day.
My family says I sing in the shower too loudly. I think I sound great.
Ha, bathrooms are the world's best concert halls. The tiles make everyone sound a little better.
So it's not just me?
Right, hard walls make sound echo, which can make your voice richer. If your family is bothered, you could sing a bit softer, or fix times when it's fine to be loud.
My friend plays piano and wants us to perform together, but I only know a few simple songs on the keyboard.
A duet doesn't need to be hard. Pick a song you both know, with an easy melody for you and a fuller part for her.
How do we practise together?
Meet once or twice a week. Start slowly, play the song through and mark the places where you lose each other. Count the beats aloud at first.
What if we make a mistake in front of people?
Keep playing and smile. Audiences usually don't notice small slips, especially if you carry on with confidence. Making a mistake together is fun too.
I'm trying to teach my dog to shake hands, but he just stares at me.
Dogs learn well with patience and treats. Do you have small treats he loves?
Yes, bits of biscuit.
Hold a treat in your closed hand near his paw. When he lifts it, even a little, say 'shake' and give him the treat. Repeat several times, and wait for a higher lift each time.
How long should I train each day?
Five minutes at a time is plenty, so he doesn't lose interest. End with a success, and he'll look forward to the next session.
He gave me his paw by accident today!
That's the start. Reward it straight away and say the word, and he'll soon connect the two.
Now he gives his paw to everyone, even the postman.
Ha, a friendly dog. It's a sweet habit. You can teach him 'wait' next, so he knows when to offer it.
My cat sits on my laptop every time I try to work. It's like she has a schedule.
Ha, cats love warm, flat places and your full attention. She might be saying, 'Look at me.'
What can I do?
Give her a warm place of her own near your desk, such as a soft blanket on a stool. A short play session before you work may tire her out.
Will she stay there?
Maybe not at first. Place a treat or her favourite toy on it, and praise her when she sits there. It takes patience, but many cats settle in time.
She sat on the blanket for five minutes. Then she went back to the laptop.
That's progress. Cats often test a new place first. Keep rewarding the blanket, and gently lift her onto it each time. In a few weeks she may adopt it.
Our dog is afraid to go down stairs. He climbs up, then just stands at the top and whines.
That's not unusual. Going down feels steeper and scarier for a dog. Is he young or old?
About three years old.
Then he's capable but nervous. Try standing a few steps below him and call him with a treat, one step at a time. Praise every small move.
What if he refuses?
Don't force him. Practise on just two steps for a few days, then add more. If he seems to be in pain or suddenly refuses, ask a vet to check on him.
I'll start with two steps.
That's a gentle plan. Keep sessions short and cheerful.
He managed all the steps on Sunday.
That's a big win. Keep praising him each time, and soon it will feel ordinary.
I'm buying a second-hand uniform for my cousin. How do I check if it's okay?
Look at the collar, cuffs and elbows, because those wear out first. Check the seams and buttons too.
What about the fit?
Ask for the size and compare it with your cousin's current one. If you can, let him try it on. A little room to grow is fine, but not too much.
What should I ask the seller?
Ask how long it was worn and whether it has been repaired. A friendly seller will tell you honestly.
The seller says it was worn for two years. Is that too long?
Two years of ordinary wear is fine if the cloth looks even and the colour hasn't faded badly. Hold it up to the light to check for thin patches.
I want to wrap a gift nicely but I don't have much money for wrapping paper.
You can make lovely wrapping from things at home. Old newspaper, brown paper bags or even a scarf can look charming.
Newspaper might look plain.
Add a ribbon or a piece of string, and a small dried flower or a hand-drawn card. A brown paper wrap with a drawing on top looks special.
I could use my drawings.
Yes. A hand-drawn pattern makes the gift feel personal. Tie it with thread or twine, and you're done.
I drew little mangoes all over it. Should I tie a ribbon?
Mangoes sound cheerful. A ribbon is a nice finishing touch, or a loop of string with a small tag bearing the name.
I need new frames for my glasses. There are so many shapes and I'm confused.
Take your time. It helps to try on several pairs. Does your optician suggest what suits your lens?
She said I can pick any shape.
Then think about comfort first. The frame shouldn't pinch behind your ears or slide down your nose. After that, choose the style and colour you like.
Round or square?

Try both and look in the mirror. Many people say that a shape that contrasts with the shape of your face looks good, but your own opinion matters most. Ask a friend or family member to say which they prefer.
I'll bring my sister along.
Good idea. A second opinion is always handy.
My sister liked the round pair. So did I.
Then it looks like you have your answer. Ask the optician to check the fit once the lenses are in.
I want to print a photo of my grandparents for their anniversary. How do I get a good print?
Use the original photo, not a screenshot, since a sharper image prints better. Do you know the size you want?
Maybe a postcard size.
A print shop can help you choose paper and size. Take the photo on a pen drive or send it from your phone, and ask them to show you a small proof first.
Should I put it in a frame?
A simple frame makes it feel special. Choose one with a plain border so the photo stands out.
The frame shop says two days, but the anniversary is tomorrow.
Then buy a ready-made frame from another shop today and fit the photo yourself, or give the print as it is with a note that the frame is coming. The thought counts.
My phone gets very hot when I play games. Is it going to explode?
Phones do warm up when working hard, but it doesn't mean it will explode. Still, heat isn't good for the battery. Is it hot to the point where you can't hold it?
Not that bad, but warm.
Take breaks, remove the cover while playing and keep it out of direct sun. If it gets very hot, stop and let it cool down. If it often overheats, ask a repair shop to check it.
I always lose track of time when I study. Can my phone help with a timer?
Yes. Try studying in blocks of twenty-five minutes, then a five-minute break. Set an alarm for each.
But my phone distracts me.
Put it in airplane mode or turn on 'do not disturb' while the timer runs, and keep it face down. Or use a simple kitchen timer if you have one.
It's a cold wave here and my school uniform isn't warm enough.
Layers help. Is your school okay with a sweater or a jacket over the uniform?
Yes, plain ones are fine.
Then wear a thin thermal layer under your shirt and a sweater on top, plus socks and a cap if allowed. Carry a scarf for the walk to school.
What about my hands?
Gloves keep them warm, and if you don't have any, keep your hands in your pockets on the way. Rub your hands together before writing.
I'll look for gloves this weekend.
Keep an old pair of socks in your bag in case you need an extra layer.
I found gloves. Should I buy one size bigger?
A little room lets a thin layer of warmth sit around your fingers, but not so loose that it's hard to hold a pencil. Try them on with your fingers fully stretched.
There was a dust storm this evening and my room is covered in a layer of dust.
That's a messy aftermath. Did the dust come in through the windows?
Yes, I left them open.
Close them during storms next time. Dust your shelves and desk with a damp cloth rather than a dry one, so the dust sticks instead of flying around, then sweep and mop the floor.
What about my books?
Wipe the covers with a slightly damp cloth, and shake the books gently. Don't wet the pages.
I'll do it tomorrow. I'm too tired tonight.
That's fine. The dust will wait, and you'll have more energy in the morning.
Should I carry an umbrella or wear a raincoat when it's windy and rainy?
A raincoat is usually better in strong wind, because an umbrella can flip inside out and be hard to hold. How are you travelling?
I walk to school.
A raincoat with a hood keeps your hands free and works well in wind. Keep your bag in a plastic cover, and wear shoes that dry quickly.
What if I only have an umbrella?
Then choose a sturdy one and hold it angled into the wind. If it's too gusty, wait for it to ease or ask someone to walk with you.
I'll go with the umbrella then. Anything else for the walk?
Wear shoes that grip wet ground, and step carefully around puddles near drains. Keep the umbrella low in the gusts.
I read aloud to my little brother at bedtime and he keeps interrupting with questions.
That's a sign he's listening. Do the questions break the story?
A bit. We never finish a chapter.
Pick a short book or a short chapter, and set a rule: you read a page, then he gets one question. That keeps the story moving and respects his curiosity.
I borrowed a library book and returned it late. Now I'm embarrassed to go back.
It happens to nearly every reader. Librarians see late returns all the time. Is there a fine?
Maybe a small one.
Then take the book back and say, 'Sorry, it's late.' Pay the fine if there is one and ask when the next due date is. Most librarians are just glad to have the book back.
We want to start a Friday family game night. Any suggestions?
Fun idea. What games does everyone enjoy?
Cards, carrom and some board games.
Rotate the choice each week, so everyone gets a turn. Add snacks and make a scoreboard for the month, with a silly prize.
What if my dad wants to win every time?
Ha, a little friendly competition is part of the fun. You can set teams, so strengths balance out. Laughing together matters more than winning.
I'll make the scoreboard tomorrow.
Great plan. Put the scoreboard on the fridge and pick a snack for the monthly winner.
I'm teaching my grandmother how to play a simple card game, and she keeps forgetting the rules.
Take it slowly and keep it playful. Which game are you teaching?
A matching game with pictures.
That's a good choice. Start by playing with the cards face up for a few rounds, so she can see everything. Say the rule in one short line before each round.
She said she's too old to learn.
You could answer, 'You taught me everything else, so now it's my turn.' Having fun together is the main thing, not the score.
That would make her smile.
I expect it will. Keep the game short and have tea afterwards.
I'm making a pookalam for Onam this year, but I'm not sure how to start.
What a cheerful tradition. Which flowers do you have?
Yellow marigolds, white jasmine and some red ones.
Sketch a circle with chalk on the floor, divide it into rings and fill each ring with a colour. Start from the centre and work outwards, pressing petals gently so they stay.
Can I make a pattern, like a star?
Yes. Mark the points of the star first with chalk, then fill the shape with one colour and the background with another. Keep the lines neat by using small petals along the edges.
The star came out lopsided.
That's easy to fix. Brush the petals aside gently and redraw the guide lines with chalk, using a ruler or string for straight edges.
We're decorating our Christmas tree with things from home instead of buying new ones.
That's creative. What do you have in mind?
Paper stars and old buttons.
Paper stars look lovely, especially if you fold them from coloured sheets. Buttons can be tied on with thread or glued onto cardboard shapes.
What about a tree topper?
A big star made from cardboard and covered in foil works well. You can also use a bow made from ribbon scraps.
We'll do the star. My sister loves foil.
Foil makes it shine nicely. Fold the edges over the back so they don't cut fingers, and glue it flat.
I'm hosting a few relatives and need to make masala chai for everyone. I only make it for myself.
Scale it up step by step. How many cups?
About six.
Boil about a cup of water per person with crushed ginger and cardamom, then add tea leaves and let them simmer. Add milk, sugar to taste and simmer once more.
Do I need to strain it?
Yes, strain it into a flask or serving pot, so the leaves don't go in the cups. Keep it warm until you're ready to serve.
I'll ask them about sugar before I add it.
Smart. Keep the sugar on the table, so people can add their own.
I have three overripe bananas. What can I do with them?
You can make banana bread, pancakes or a smoothie. Overripe bananas are sweeter, which is perfect for baking.
Which is the easiest?
A smoothie, since you only need milk and the bananas. For something to eat later, mash them and mix with flour for simple pancakes.
My friend is changing schools next month, and I'm sad about it.
That's hard news. It's okay to feel sad. Do you know how you'll keep in touch?
Probably messages and calls.
That's a good start. You could also plan a visit, or set a regular call. Before she leaves, make a small memory, like a photo or a card.
I made a photo collage last week.
She'll love it. You've already done something special. Keep a few pictures for yourself too.
I will. Thanks.
A change like this is tough, but good friends find ways to stay close.
My friend got through her exams and we want to surprise her with a small celebration.
That's a lovely idea. What does she like?
Chocolate cake and board games.
Then a small party with cake and her favourite games sounds perfect. Invite two or three close friends and keep it simple.
How do we keep it a secret?
Ask a friend to invite her out at a set time and bring her to the party. Keep the planning on a separate chat she isn't in.
We'll tell her it's a study session.
That should work. Have the cake ready and the lights low before she arrives.
Our building wants to start a compost bin, but I'm not sure what goes in.
Compost likes fruit and vegetable peels, tea leaves, eggshells and dry leaves. What do you have in mind?
Kitchen scraps, mostly.
Mix wet scraps with dry material like leaves or shredded paper to avoid a bad smell. Avoid cooked food, oil and meat, which can attract pests.
How long does it take?
Usually a few months, depending on the weather and how often you turn it. When it looks like dark soil and smells earthy, it's ready for your plants.
Is it okay to add banana peels? We have loads.
Yes, banana peels are good for compost. Chop them small so they break down faster, and mix them with dry leaves.
Why is the sky red at sunset?
At sunset, sunlight passes through more air to reach your eyes. The air scatters blue light away, so what's left is mostly red and orange.
So the colours were always in the sunlight?
Yes, sunlight contains all colours mixed together. At midday, the blue scatters across the sky and makes it blue. At sunset the long path leaves the warm colours.
I'm giving a short speech at the morning assembly and I'm nervous.
That's a big stage, but a short speech is manageable. What's the topic?
Kindness.
A good topic. Tell one small story about a kind thing you saw, say why it mattered and end with a one-line message. Keep it under two minutes.
Should I memorise it?
Know the main points well, and carry a card with key words. Reading word for word can sound stiff, but a quick glance at the card helps you keep track.
I'll practise in front of my family tonight.
Ask them to sit at the far end of the room, so you practise speaking loudly enough.
My classmate keeps borrowing my pencils and never returns them.
That's annoying when you have to keep buying new ones. Have you mentioned it to him?
Not yet.
You could say, 'I need my pencils back, so please return them by the end of the day.' A friendly but clear request is fair.
What if he forgets again?
Carry only one spare pencil, and lend it only on the understanding that it comes back. A pencil case with a few labelled ones also helps.
I told him, and he said sorry and returned four pencils!
That's a great result. A clear, kind request often works. Thank him for returning them, and everyone's happy.
I want to improve my basketball dribbling, but I keep losing the ball.
Dribbling improves with practice. Are you looking at the ball while you dribble?
Yes, all the time.
Try keeping your head up and use your fingertips, not your palm. Start by dribbling in place, then walk, then jog. Practise with both hands.
How often should I practise?
Fifteen minutes a day will help a lot. Keep it varied, with figure eights, zigzags and cone drills. Your coach can suggest more.
I just started swimming backstroke, and water keeps going up my nose.
That's very common. Are you keeping your head still?
I don't think so. I keep lifting it.
Keep your head resting back in the water with your eyes looking up, and breathe out through your nose gently as you move. That stops water from entering.
On long train journeys I always want the window seat, and my sister always gets it. We argue every time.
Ha, a classic. Is there an easy way to be fair?
Not really. She says she's younger.
Try taking turns by journey, or by halves of the trip. You could also swap at a particular station, which makes it a game.
What if she refuses?
You could suggest a coin toss before each journey, so the decision is fair and quick. Or ask a parent to settle the rule once, so you don't argue each time.
We're going on a road trip and I'm in charge of snacks. What should I pack?
Choose things that don't melt or crumble too much. What does everyone like?
Chips, biscuits and fruit.
Add roasted nuts, dry fruit and a few packs of plain crackers. Carry water, and some wet wipes for sticky fingers.
What about something for the kids?
Small fruit like grapes or cut apple slices in a box, and mild biscuits. Avoid very messy items in the car.
I'll make a snack bag for each person.
Great idea. Label the bags to avoid arguments about whose is whose.
I'd like to ask my colleague for feedback on my report, but I'm afraid of criticism.
Asking for feedback is a mature step. Which colleague are you thinking of?
Someone senior, who's kind but honest.
That sounds like a good choice. Ask a specific question, like, 'Is the summary clear?' It helps them give useful comments.
What if the feedback is negative?
Listen, take notes and say thank you. You can think it over later and decide what to change. Feedback is about the work, not about you.
My team lead asked everyone to send a weekly update, and I never know what to write.
A weekly update can be short. Think in three parts: what you finished, what you're working on and anything you need help with.
What if I finished almost nothing?
Then be honest and say what you worked on, even if it isn't done. For example, 'I made progress on the report and will finish it by Tuesday.'
I have to recite a poem on Monday and the words keep slipping out of my head.
Try learning two lines at a time instead of the whole poem. Say them aloud, look away, and say them again from memory. Add the next two lines only when the first two feel easy.
I know the first stanza now. Should I go on tonight or wait until tomorrow?

Go on a little tonight, then get a good night's sleep. Sleep helps memory settle, so the first stanza will probably still be there in the morning. Do a quick run-through of it before you start the new lines.
My little cousin says she hates vegetables, and we're making lunch together tomorrow.
Cooking together is a good start. Children often try food they helped make, so let her wash, tear or stir while you do the cutting.
She likes anything crunchy. Does that help?
It helps a lot. Crunchy options like cucumber or carrot sticks could suit her, and she can pick the crunchiest one herself.
She chose cucumber! Any easy way to serve it?
Good pick. Cut it into thin sticks and add a little salt and lemon, or roll slices inside a roti. Serve it first, while she is hungry and curious.
My younger brother just lost his first tooth and he's very proud. How can I make it feel special?
What a milestone. You could let him tell the story of how it came out, and take a photo of his new gap-toothed smile. Little rituals make it fun.
He's asking if the tooth fairy is real.
That is a tricky one. You could ask him what he thinks first, since children often have their own ideas. Then you can follow your parents' lead, because it is their family story to tell.
Good idea, I'll ask Mom. He wants to keep the tooth, though.
That's fine. A small box or an empty matchbox-sized container with a label and the date works well. He can look at it when he's older and smile.
Thanks! He's already picked a box.
Then the plan is complete. A proud brother, a box, and a story. Enjoy the gap-toothed grins.
I have to wear a tie for an interview and I've never tied one.
It's a skill you can learn in one evening. Look for a step-by-step picture or video, and practise with the tie on a chair back first, so you are not rushing in front of the mirror.
I tried but one end is always much longer than the other.

That is common at the start. The wide end should hang a little lower than the narrow end, so begin with the wide end well below the narrow one and adjust from there. A few tries will show you the right starting point.
Got it. Should I practise a few times before the day?
Yes, three or four tries on separate evenings will help. By interview day, your hands will remember the steps and you can think about the conversation instead.
I'll do that. Any advice for the first minute of the interview?
Smile, say good morning, and give a firm but friendly hello. Keep your first answer short and clear. A calm start sets the tone for the rest.
My friend Kabir is always late. Yesterday I waited forty minutes at the cinema.
That sounds frustrating, especially standing around waiting. Does he usually have a reason, or does he just lose track of time?
He loses track of time. He's not being rude, I think.
Then a friendly chat may work. You could say you enjoy meeting him but waiting is hard for you, and ask how you can both plan better.
Is a money plant easy to grow in a glass jar? I'd like to try one.
Yes, it is a good plant for beginners. Put a cutting with a node, the small bump on the stem, in the water, and keep the jar in bright light but out of strong direct sun.
How often should I change the water?
Every week or so is fine, or sooner if it looks cloudy. Fresh water gives the roots what they need.
Roots have started to show! When can I move it to soil?
When the roots are a few centimetres long, you can plant it in a small pot with ordinary garden soil. Water it lightly after planting, and don't be alarmed if a leaf droops for a day or two.
Grandpa's birthday is coming and I'd like to make him a card, but I can't draw well.
Handmade cards don't need good drawing. Your words matter more than the pictures, and he will love that you made it for him.
What could I write inside?
Write a real memory, such as a walk you took together or a story he told you. Finish with a short wish like, 'I hope your year is full of tea, sunshine and good company.'
I like that. Should I decorate the front with leaves from the garden?
Pressed leaves look lovely. Let them dry between the pages of a heavy book for a day or two first, then glue them on lightly.
Perfect, he loves the garden. He's turning seventy.
Then maybe write a big seven and a zero on the front, and let the leaves form a border around them. That makes a card he can show off to visitors.
I'm bad at carrom. My cousins always beat me.
Carrom is a game where small changes help a lot. Which part goes wrong: hitting the coin, or aiming?
Both, honestly. The striker slides off the coin.
